analysis.one_liner: Bans most unwanted automated robocalls and requires phone companies to verify caller ID.
analysis.headline: The anti-robocall bill never left committee: referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on June 7, 2018, it drew two cosponsors and received no hearing or vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have cracked down on unwanted automated phone calls and texts — "robocalls." It would have tightened the definition of an illegal robocall, let people revoke consent to be called at any time, created a national database of reassigned phone numbers so callers stop bothering the wrong people, extended the time limit for federal penalties against violators to four years, and required phone companies to verify caller ID so scammers can't fake numbers — at no extra charge to customers. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who owns a phone. The bill would have made most automated calls and texts — "robocalls" — illegal without tighter consent rules, let people revoke consent to be called at any time and in any reasonable way, and required that even calls currently exempt from the rules (like certain government or informational calls) carry a way to opt out [S2][S3]. It would have created a national database of reassigned phone numbers so callers stop dialing numbers that now belong to someone else, extended the time limit for the FCC to penalize violators to four years, and required phone companies to verify caller ID so scammers can't fake numbers — at no extra charge to customers [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: It rewrites the law's definition of a robocall to cover equipment that dials lists of stored numbers or randomly generated numbers, closing gaps that let automated callers argue their equipment fell outside the existing ban.
It gives consumers a clear right to revoke consent to be called at any time and in any reasonable manner, rather than being locked into whatever fine-print consent they gave.
It requires the FCC to attach real protections to the categories of calls currently exempt from the robocall ban, including limits on who can be called, how often, and a mandatory opt-out mechanism.
It orders a nationwide database of reassigned phone numbers, with safe-harbor rules, so callers who act in good faith stop dialing numbers that have been handed to new subscribers.

It extends the statute of limitations for robocall and caller ID violations to four years and removes the requirement of a prior citation before seeking FCC fines, giving regulators more time and a clearer path to penalize violators.
It requires voice service providers to implement caller ID authentication technology that verifies numbers and blocks unverified spoofed calls, and bars them from charging subscribers extra for it.

It requires the FCC to report to Congress annually on robocall complaints, enforcement actions, and penalties collected, including an analysis of providers that carry high volumes of short-duration robocall traffic.

analysis.who_pays: Telemarketing and robocall operations would bear the cost of restrictions and larger penalties (a four-year window for FCC fines instead of the general limit) [S3]. Voice service providers would have to build and run caller ID verification technology and report reassigned numbers to a national database, and would be barred from charging subscribers extra for the verification technology [S3]. Businesses that call customers with automated systems would face tighter rules on getting and keeping consent [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill applies to far more than scammers: hospitals, pharmacies, schools, and other businesses that legitimately use automated appointment and reminder calls would have faced tighter consent rules, limits on call volume, and mandatory opt-out systems, raising their compliance costs.

The carve-out for equipment that requires 'substantial additional human intervention' is a fuzzy standard that would have invited litigation over which callers qualify, recreating in new form the definitional fights the bill was written to settle.

The mandate that phone companies implement caller ID authentication at no additional charge to subscribers pushes compliance costs onto the providers, who could recover them through general rate increases rather than a labeled fee.

The reassigned-number database imposes reporting duties on every covered voice and text provider and shifts to them the risk of database errors, since inaccuracies they report are a condition of callers' safe harbor.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits would have gone to tens of millions of phone users who receive billions of unwanted and fraudulent automated calls each year, through fewer robocalls, verified caller ID, easier consent revocation, and longer enforcement windows. The costs fall mainly on the telemarketing industry whose business the bill restricts, and secondarily on phone companies through technology mandates and on legitimate businesses that use automated reminders. The main design weakness is the vague human-intervention carve-out, which could have produced years of litigation, and the burden the bill places on legitimate automated callers alongside scammers. On balance, the consumer protections are substantial and the costs are real but narrower.

outcome.mechanism: It went to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and sat there until the two-year Congress ended, without ever getting a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr. introduced the bill on June 7, 2018, late in the two-year session of the 115th Congress.
The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the same day and never moved from there.
The action record shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote at any point before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
The bill drew only two cosponsors, both Democrats, so it entered the session's final months with minimal visible support.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Telemarketers and robocall operations, which kept calling under the pre-existing rules, and phone companies, which faced no new verification or database mandates. Consumers kept receiving unwanted and fraudulent automated calls.

for.name: Frank Pallone Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 7, 2018, writing the robocall restrictions and FCC mandates it contained

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and took no further action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress

against.name: Greg Walden
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee where the bill sat, never scheduled it for consideration; committee action records show no markup was ever held

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; the bill's only support on the record came from Democrats — the sponsor and two Democratic cosponsors.

industries.note: The bill targets the core business of mass automated calling: it broadens the definition of illegal robocalls, tightens consent rules, and lengthens the penalty window to four years. Its gain would have come directly at the expense of people receiving unwanted calls.

Providers would have had to implement caller ID authentication technology and report reassigned numbers to a national database, with the bill barring them from charging subscribers extra for it. But the same bill gives them a safe harbor from robocall liability if they query the database in good faith, protecting them from suits over reassigned numbers.

industries.industry: Businesses using automated customer calls (banks, appointment reminders, delivery notifications)
industries.note: The expanded robocall definition and stricter consent rules would have covered any business dialing customers automatically, raising costs and legal exposure for outreach many consumers find useful.
